prize_parts.citation: for showing how technology and trade shocks reshape labour demand, wages and local labour markets

statement.case_for: B032 pairs a conceptual account of how tasks and technology shape labour demand with transparent, credibly identified quasi-experimental evidence on import competition and local labour-market adjustment. That pairing of data and design with an explanatory framework is what I weigh most heavily. The scientific effect is large. It changed how economists model polarisation and the distributional costs of trade, and it has produced a large follow-on literature with its own replications, critiques and refinements. The core papers span roughly 2003 to 2016, so they have had time to be scrutinised, and the main qualitative findings have held up even where magnitudes are debated. After reading colleagues' openings I am moving from Autor-Hanson-Katz to Autor-Hanson-Dorn. The shift-share exposure design and the local labour-market evidence are a joint Autor-Dorn-Hanson contribution, and most colleagues who ranked B032 name Dorn. Katz's central work on skill premia and the race between education and technology is a distinct strand. It also sits close to the 2023 prize, where Goldin and Katz were co-authors on that theme.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that B032 may combine two contributions: the task framework, whose theory also rests on people outside the credited list such as Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu and Restrepo, and the China-shock evidence. A three-name award therefore risks an incomplete attribution of the framework side. Magnitude, persistence and inference in exposure-based designs remain contested. The 2024 prize on technology and institutions and the recent labour-economics prizes (Card, Angrist and Imbens, Goldin) mean the Committee may see the area as already well recognised. Katz is left out of this configuration, and that is a real cost to credit.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B014 first. He argues that Calvo's pricing and Taylor's contracts and rule, together with Woodford's synthesis, underpin modern monetary policy. He also says the cluster is crowded and that a three-name limit leaves out major contributors such as Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets.
responses.response: I agree that B014 has the broadest policy footprint. I place it below B032 because the attribution problem he describes is severe. Eight credited names, several distinct strands and Gertler's overlap with other ballots mean any trio omits people with strong claims. His point that the 2021-23 inflation episode revived debate about the framework also tempers my confidence, though I accept it does not undermine the original contributions. B032's credit is also contested, but Autor, Hanson and Dorn are identifiable co-originators of a single empirical programme. I keep B014 as an alternative, not my preferred part.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B032 first with Autor and Hanson. She stresses transparent empirical designs, replication and re-examination, and policy influence. She also says Dorn or Katz might be favoured over Hanson.
responses.response: I agree that the transparent design and the record of re-examination make B032 mature enough to lead. I diverge on the cut. I would not drop Dorn. He is a co-originator of the local labour-market design, and Autor-Dorn-Hanson is the cleanest unit of attribution. A two-person award would leave out a core co-author. I also do not see Dorn displacing Hanson. The trio is more faithful to the evidence, and the three-name limit allows it.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B042 first. He argues that Kiyotaki and Moore's 1997 credit-cycles paper is a clean, foundational mechanism. He proposes only the two originators because the financial-accelerator strand is tied to Bernanke, who is not on the list. He also notes the possible overlap with the 2022 prize.
responses.response: I agree the Kiyotaki-Moore attribution is tighter than in most candidates and is a strong alternative. His reasoning also makes me doubt my own opening proposal to add Gertler. Bernanke's 2022 recognition makes the accelerator lineage hard to split, and the two-person core is cleaner. My remaining hesitation is that the mechanism is better established as theory than through direct identification of the collateral channel. The overlap with the 2022 prize on banking and financial crises also remains unresolved. I would not go beyond Kiyotaki and Moore if the Committee prefers B042.

responses.point: Hassler lists B032 sixth with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. He notes that task-approach credit is shared with Acemoglu, already a laureate, and Katz, and that some China-shock findings are debated on magnitude and persistence.
responses.response: This is a fair qualification and I take it seriously. It is why I would frame the citation around the labour-market effects of technology and trade shocks, with the China-shock evidence as the identified core, and not claim the whole task-based theory. The Acemoglu overlap is real but partial. Acemoglu's recognised work concerns institutions and prosperity, and the empirical local-adjustment evidence is a separate contribution. The debate over persistence concerns magnitudes and does not remove the qualitative finding that import-competition shocks have lasting local labour-market costs.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats the task framework and the trade-shock evidence as one contribution or two, and whether the framework's theoretical credit outside the credited names (Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu, Restrepo) undermines a three-person award.
Whether Katz or Dorn is the better third name. I have chosen Dorn on attribution grounds, but this is a judgement call.
The long-run magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects, and the validity of shift-share inference.
How the Committee weighs recent recognition of labour and technology topics (Card, Angrist and Imbens, Goldin, Acemoglu) against the merits of this contribution.
The relative priority of B042 and B014 if the Committee prefers a macroeconomic award. B014's attribution is diffuse, and B042 overlaps thematically with the 2022 prize.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. None of the credited names on B032 (Autor, Hanson, Dorn, Katz) appears among her listed frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler). Her field proximity to labour economics and her 2023 committee entry alongside the Goldin prize are disclosed as context, not as a documented conflict.
